title: Bridging the Gap Between Techlash and Instructional Redesign
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky diagnoses a widening gap between two conversations about technology in schools that never speak to each other: a popular 'techlash' giving voice to real discontent, and the instructional-design work of AI educators who respond with assignment redesign, metacognitive checkpoints, and rubric revision. He argues the discontent is about far more than screens — stalled AI returns, fear of automation, and a diffuse sense of powerlessness — and that school technology, like the opposed data center, has become the physical address where that grievance can acquire a public comment period and a vote. The problem, he says, is one of altitude: the field answers structural grievance with instructional design because design is the register its trained optimism knows how to act in, and that answer keeps failing to land. Surveying six candidates for a genuine 'third response' — digital wellness, attention as a curricular object, transparency, agency and authorship, shared governance, and institutional patience — he concludes none is clean, and any candidate that claims to resolve the problem has probably already been absorbed.
points: Two 'stacks' of reading — the techlash critique and the daily flood of AI-literacy frameworks — do not speak to each other, and that gap is the central problem of the field.
The discontent is about much more than screens: 40% of workers fear losing their job to automation, and school technology becomes the place diffuse anxiety can land.
Potkalitsky calls this 'The Altitude Problem': the field answers structural grievance (pay, workload, top-down decisions) with instructional design, the only register its optimism knows.
Unlike prior hype-disappointment cycles, this backlash 'has left the building' — statehouse legislation in at least 17 states and a $1.6 billion contract audit in Los Angeles.

He lays out six candidate 'third responses' — wellness, attention, transparency, agency/authorship, shared governance, and institutional patience — and warns any clean-seeming solution risks being absorbed by one side.
quotes: I keep picking up one stack and setting down the other, and the gap between them is starting to feel like the central problem of this field.
The Digital Delusion did not create the discontent now directed at education technology. It gave that discontent a vocabulary it could carry into a school board meeting.
And school technology has become one of those places, the site where frustration about capital, attention, and powerlessness can acquire a public comment period and a vote.
The data center is where the grievance goes when it needs a physical address. The Chromebook cart works the same way.
The field answers structural grievance with instructional design because design is the register in which its trained optimism knows how to act.
What is different now is that the backlash has statehouse legislation in at least 17 states and a $1.6 billion contract audit in Los Angeles. It has left the building.
I do not think any single candidate here resolves the problem I have been describing. I think any candidate that claims to has probably already been absorbed.
